item.title: The Roles of Mind, Self, and Brain in Healing Depression: Learning to Stay Out of the River of Our Negative Cognitions
item.description:
Depression occurs when stressful life events influence the brain. These events create more negative thoughts and feelings and more distortion in the way the brain processes information. To understand this process is it is important to realize that the human brain consists of three distinct components which have a role in the management of depression.

Three Components of Depression Management

The first component, which we will identify, is the mind, located in the anterior cingulate gyrus. The mind is the stream or river of consciousness through which flow thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. It is not the source of the content of the river; it is a conduit for processing the content.

The second component is the Self, located in the prefrontal cortex, on the bank of the mind or river of consciousness. This component is our sense of “I”, the internal executor of the brain, and in a real sense, this is where our soul resides, called our “heart” in the Scriptures.

The Self could observe the thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations which flow through the mind and process them. The Self observes the contents of the river, but they are not the same as the mind.

Just because a thought enters the river, it doesn’t mean you have to believe it – the Self determines the validity of the contents of the river. The limbic system of the brain is the source of the contents of the river – thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. Remember, the brain is not the same component as the mind.

How the Brain Processes Information

The brain produces the stream of thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations by processing information from:

  • The real world
  • Your body and senses, including your gut
  • By recalling past packages of thoughts, feelings, beliefs, and motor/action plans or schemas that make sense of our experiences

For example, you see a plant while on a hike, and you’ve never seen one like it before. It might be a green leafy plant, but you’ve never seen this kind before. What is it? The automatic systems in your brain take over and process this real-world information with the anxiety you are feeling in your body and gut, as you are concerned this might actually be poison ivy, because you have heard there might be some around.

The brain then starts recalling things from your past. This plant has three leaves like the one you touched when you were a kid, so it sends anxiety and danger signals down the river. But these automatic functions only control 80% of your brain. The other 5-20 % come from the Self. So, you have some executor options. You can become overwhelmed by what the brain is sending, believe it, and jump in the river, or you can analyze and appraise.

You can say things like, yes, there might be poison ivy plants around, but they do not have leaves like the one I saw as a kid. Yes, poison ivy can cause problems, but didn’t that plant hurt me when I was a kid because I plucked it up? Have any of my friends had a problem with poison ivy on this trail?

The Brain and the Self

The brain is an organ, just like the gut or the heart. Sometimes it cooperates fully with the rest of the body, and sometimes it doesn’t. If you allow negative things into your brain, i.e., pornography, violent video games or movies, abuse, it will react negatively. You are not your brain, but you can change your brain.

Negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations sent into the river by the brain are observed by the Self, which is safely located on the bank in the real world, where it can reappraise after stepping back and seeing the situation clearly.

The problem develops when the Self becomes entangled in the river by ruminating on the thoughts and feelings it encounters there. You (Self) become the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations. This rumination results in a new reality. The Self, who is stuck in the river, creates a new thought: “My brain is telling me this, so it must be true!”

The result of this new reality is an overwhelming sense of sadness, lack of motivation, and loss of interest in things we formerly enjoyed. The Self is stuck in negative thoughts. One of the consequences of the Self being stuck in the river is that the prefrontal cortex is turned off and is not working as designed. The solution to the problem lies in learning to redirect attention to the real world through mindfulness techniques and cognitive restructuring.

Mindfulness

Mindfulness is keeping our thoughts in the present, where it is safe, and not in the past, which is dominated by “If onlys”, or the future, which is dominated by “What ifs.” Cognitive restructuring is challenging the validity and logic of the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, using the logical prefrontal cortex where the Self resides.

The safest place to direct attention is to the real world, not the river. If we fall into the river, we drown in depression. So, the question you need to ask yourself is, “Is there anything happening right here, right now in this room with which you cannot deal or handle?”

Healing depression focuses on climbing out of the river by remembering the scriptural admonition to claim the promise of Philippians 4:7, and receive the peace of God, which the Apostle Paul states, “…Surpasses all understanding, and will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Phil. 4:7 ESV).

If we can learn not to live in the past or worry about the future, but instead to learn from the past and apply the lessons learned, we can face the future assured of the strength of the Lord to guide us. And in the process, we allow the Self to resume the executor role of the brain as God designed it, and we stay grounded in the present in the real world.

Research has shown that the Brain has the capacity to stay in the present for 4-7 seconds before it starts to wander to the past or future. Consequently, we need to empower the Self, steal that attention away from the brain, and mindfully bring it back to the present.

We accomplish this with in-the-moment coping skills, such as diaphragmatic breathing, mindfulness techniques that activate prefrontal cortex activity, and challenging the validity and logic of negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations.

Challenging Negative Thoughts

We can systematically challenge each negative thought, each negative feeling, each troubling image, and each sensation by identifying what percentage they are true. At first, we might think they are 90-100% true, and that’s what keeps us in the river. But the Self, which is watching from the riverbank, can see that the reality is that the percentage is much, much lower. A common example is “I can never do anything right!” and it is believed 100%.

But hearing the Self challenge the statement with the logic that no one is always wrong, and everyone does some things right, lowers the percentage substantially and starts on the path to healing. Allowing the Self to put the negatives on trial, and asking, “What is the evidence that I should believe this?”, is another effective way to climb out of the river.

In conclusion, don’t forget that living in the “If onlys” of the past and the “What ifs” of the future will cause the brain to convince us that there is no hope. When we get the Self and the prefrontal cortex involved in the challenging process, we can claim the promise that healing and peace are only a prayer away!

So, if you feel you are drowning in the river of your negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, please know there is hope through a therapist who understands the healing process. Please check our website and make an appointment today. Peace awaits.

Reference:
Gary A. Sibcy II, P. (2021). Clinical Depression: Evidence-based Counseling Treatment and Strategies. CounselTalk Webinar. Lynchburg, VA: Liberty University.

item.title: What is Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?
item.description:
We have all seen it before – a social media friend posts a picture of their perfectly color-coded closet. Their pantry is organized into matching containers. Every towel is folded exactly the same way. The caption reads: “#OCD.”

Or maybe you’ve seen someone look at a crooked picture frame or a stack of papers that isn’t perfectly straight and joke, “My OCD is going so crazy right now.” Most of us have laughed, nodded, or kept scrolling without thinking much about it.

But what if OCD is actually something completely different? What if the person silently battling Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder has a messy closet, an overflowing laundry basket, and a mind that never gives them a moment of peace?

The truth is that OCD has little to do with being neat, organized, or particular. It is a disorder driven by fear. It is a disorder built on uncertainty. And for those living with it, it can feel like you are battling a monster on steroids every single day.

Why OCD Thoughts Cause So Much Distress

One of the most difficult parts of OCD is that people often mistake intrusive thoughts for who they are.

An intrusive thought is exactly what it sounds like: an unwanted thought, image, or urge that repeatedly barges into your mind without your permission. These thoughts are distressing because they are the exact thoughts you do not want to have. If you could snap your fingers and make them disappear forever, you would.

Ironically, the harder you try to force them away, argue with them, or prove they are not true, the longer they tend to stick around. This is one of the reasons OCD is so exhausting. These types of thoughts are often referred to as “sticky thoughts” (also referred to as obsessions).

Everyone experiences random intrusive thoughts from time to time. A person who isn’t battling OCD may briefly notice the thought and move on with their day. Their brain simply lets it pass.

But someone dealing with OCD tends to get stuck. The thought lingers, replaying over and over. It may stay for hours or even days, demanding attention and creating tremendous anxiety. The brain becomes convinced that the thought must mean something important simply because it won’t leave.

People might think:

“What if I secretly want this?”
“What if this thought means something about me?”
“What if God is trying to tell me something?”
“What if everyone else is safe except me?”

However, the opposite is usually true. OCD likes to attack what matters most to us. A loving mother may develop terrifying thoughts about accidentally harming her child. A devoted Christian might become consumed with fears that they have committed an unforgivable sin or will in the future.

A compassionate person may become terrified that they could harm someone else, or even themselves, despite desperately not wanting to. Someone who deeply values honesty becomes trapped wondering if they lied without realizing it.

Deep down, people battling with OCD might even recognize that these thoughts are attacking the values they hold most dear. If a thought fills you with fear because it goes completely against who you are and what you believe, that is often evidence that it is not something you actually want to do. OCD doesn’t reveal your character. Instead, it attacks your values.

Could I be dealing with OCD?

If you’ve been reading this article and wondering whether this could apply to you, here are some common symptoms of OCD.

OCD may be the culprit if you:

  • Experience recurring intrusive thoughts, images, or urges that feel unwanted and distressing.
  • Spend a significant amount of time trying to figure out what your thoughts mean.
  • Constantly seek reassurance from others that everything is okay.
  • Feel driven to check, repeat, confess, avoid, or perform mental rituals to reduce anxiety.
  • Feel temporary relief after completing a compulsion, only to have the fear return later.
  • Find yourself avoiding people, places, objects, or situations that trigger intrusive thoughts.
  • Spend an hour or more each day consumed by obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors.
  • Notice that the anxiety is interfering with your work, relationships, parenting, school, or ability to enjoy life.

It is important to remember that everyone experiences intrusive thoughts from time to time. Having an intrusive thought does not necessarily mean you are dealing with OCD. The difference is how your brain responds to the thought. For someone who isn’t fighting OCD, the thought usually comes and goes without much attention.

For someone who is facing OCD, the thought can become “sticky.” The brain treats it like an emergency that must be solved immediately. This is where compulsions may develop. But, the more you try to make the thought go away, the stronger it often becomes. This only makes the cycles stronger.

If this cycle sounds familiar, know that you are not alone. OCD affects millions of people, and many go years before receiving an accurate diagnosis because they don’t realize what they’re experiencing has a name.

There is hope

If you recognized yourself in this article, know that OCD is highly treatable. You do not have to stay trapped in the exhausting cycle of obsessions (sticky thoughts) and/or compulsions (behaviors you adopt to relieve the anxiety you feel).

Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a specialized form of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), is the gold-standard treatment for OCD. Rather than trying to eliminate intrusive thoughts, ERP helps you change your response to them so they gradually lose their power.

Recovery doesn’t mean you’ll never have another intrusive thought. It means those thoughts no longer control your life.

If you’re struggling with OCD or intrusive thoughts, I’d love to help. Reach out today to schedule an appointment and learn how evidence-based treatment can help you break free from OCD and regain peace.

item.title: How Emotionally-Focused Marriage Therapy Can Help Couples Facing Chronic Disease
item.description:
For someone dealing with a sudden diagnosis or finally discovering what’s beneath their health issues, chronic disease is difficult. Whether the newly diagnosed person receives the news in a way that alters their self-perception or it is slowly revealed through life’s limitations, chronic health issues take their toll. Not only is it hard for the individual experiencing them, but they can be damaging to a marriage.

If you or someone you love is dealing with chronic illness or a new diagnosis that impacts the rest of their life, it may be wise to seek emotionally focused marriage therapy as another tool for your well-being toolkit.

Here’s why:

Marriages facing additional layers of complexity need more complex layers of support. Marriage is hard no matter what. But when one partner is diagnosed with a life-threatening illness or a disease that significantly impacts the family, it adds more stress to the relationship. With about 41% of first marriages ending in divorce, even without chronic health issues, it’s important to arm yourself with as many wellness tools as you can.

What is emotionally focused marriage therapy?

According to the International Center for Excellence in Emotionally Focused Therapy (ICEEFT), couples counseling rooted in emotionally focused therapy takes “an evidence-based approach to psychotherapy, drawing primarily from attachment theory to facilitate the creation of secure, vibrant connection with self and others.”

It’s a means of helping couples identify where they’re attached insecurely, learn new ways of attaching to one another that bring life and health back to the marriage, and approach problem-solving and plans from the emotionally focused lens they’ve developed in their sessions.

Emotionally focused marriage therapy has three phases: De-escalation, Restructuring, and Consolidation.

In de-escalation, a couple explores what “broke” the healthy attachments they once had. If they didn’t develop these healthy attachments, they will explore what might contribute to that. Often, there are cycles that a couple can recognize that explain why they have had the same fight for years and didn’t know how to solve it.

With restructuring, a couple learns new ways to listen, be open to each other, and express their needs. Both partners can be available to the other person’s needs in a way that feels authentic yet invites vulnerability. This builds a foundation of trust and safety that the lack of attachment did not previously contain.

The third phase, consolidation, helps the couple recognize how their new tools can be useful in the future. Particularly with couples facing chronic illness, this phase is crucial to helping them reflect on ways they can partner together to use the therapeutic listening and engaging they’ve learned as they cope with the emotional upheaval that chronic illness can create.

How can this therapy help us with chronic health diagnoses?

When one partner receives life-changing health news, it’s challenging to embrace. But then, the steady impact over time becomes a “new normal” that their spouse needs to receive, and if not, this can disrupt the marital connection.

It can also create levels of feeling unseen or unsupported, especially if the partner with the illness doesn’t feel cared for. No matter how much their spouse wants to show support, they may simply not be equipped to show it in a way that communicates support the way their partner needs.

Even doctors miss this sometimes, so it’s natural that a spouse trying to support their spouse who’s facing chronic health issues may not know how to do it well. Emotions run high on both sides, fear can enter the picture even for the most confident couples, and security may go out the proverbial window.

So, a counselor trained in emotionally focused marriage therapy can be a godsend to couples who just don’t know what to do next. They’ve made the physical health decisions (or some of them anyway) about medications, treatments, and lifestyle changes. But when it comes to the emotional side of it? That’s a layer that can feel too burdensome to tackle with the physical health decisions as well.

Your EFT counselor will help by letting you practice the therapy in the actual sessions. He or she will guide you through each phase, so you can see that you don’t have to “do” anything except listen to the counselor, talk honestly, and have a willing heart. A willingness to understand your spouse during this stressful time goes a long way.

In counseling, you’ll learn the ineffective ways your communication, expression of emotions, and actions toward each other impact the relationship’s harmony and sense of safety. The counselor will also teach you how to recognize your feelings, fears, and anything else serving as barriers to connection to each other during this season.

An Example of How EFT Fuels Conversation in Couple Therapy

Here’s an example from one research study about how a cancer patient’s diagnosis can move from panic and stress-inducing to peaceful and comfort-building in their relationship. Let’s suppose one partner is diagnosed with cancer.

When the shock of the diagnosis has subsided somewhat, the person’s partner may want to discuss treatment options, what-if scenarios, and how to maximize support. The partner may be so fearful of outcomes that they avoid these discussions.

The success of those conversations (or avoidances) can have a direct impact on emotional health. Still, some studies show that even a person’s physical recovery time can be reduced if their partner can provide the kind of support they need.

A counselor who specializes in emotionally focused couple therapy may meet with the couple to discern (in phase one) which cycles are playing a role in their discussions about the newfound diagnosis. Through a conversation they have in session, a counselor may gently ask a reflective question to the person experiencing the illness: How does it make you feel when you talk about cancer and your spouse changes the subject?

The couple can practice navigating their feelings, being open with one another, and learning (with the counselor’s guidance) to listen to each other’s needs with empathy. Over time, this transitions them to phase two, where the learned experience transforms how they provide support to one another.

What they discover, then, is that they each have significant needs; no one partner’s needs are “more important” than the other. That way, they learn how to value one another’s feelings, express themselves with gentleness, and receive feedback so they can talk more openly and with kindness, compassion, and even humor.

Couples who navigate through health challenges with these communication styles tend to walk away from the challenges feeling more connected to their partner than before.

While emotionally focused therapy doesn’t focus on skill development like cognitive behavioral therapy would, it does incorporate learning in a flexible, felt-need way. This fluid approach to seeing and hearing each other in therapy sessions with a guide can provide a sense of comfort to the partner who may be resistant to therapy at first.

What to Expect in Emotionally Focused Marriage Therapy Session One

First, recognize that it is common not to want to attend therapy. Usually at least one partner – if not both – is hesitant. Hesitation can come from a host of attitudes, feelings, and beliefs about what marriage therapy involves.

Second, both partners should be aware that the first session is not a long-term commitment. You’re simply going to share what fueled the idea. It’s not a blame game; it’s pragmatics. One of you was diagnosed with a chronic illness or disease, and you’d like a little help navigating how you’re both coping with the news. It can be simple and fact-driven. You don’t need to be ready to bear your soul or even understand how you’re feeling.

Third, the counselor who specializes in emotionally focused marriage therapy understands not just how to ask questions but also how to hold space for someone who may be grieving, disassociated from what’s happening, feeling ignored or left out, or a variety of other hard realities.

If anything, a counselor looking at therapy from an EFT lens will be more inclined to affirm where you are right now. You’ll walk away with hope – and that’s often reason enough to attend just one session.

Finally, it can be a mutual decision after you’ve attended session one about whether you think it will benefit you both. Listening to the counselor and sharing a bit of your story from an overview level won’t repair anyone overnight; however, it can give you an idea of whether you’ll each get something out of a second session.

If you or your spouse, or someone else in your lives, would benefit from emotionally focused marriage therapy, we are here for you. Contact one of our offices to be matched with a counselor in your area.

item.title: Signs and Symptoms of Perimenopause and How Your Husband Can Provide Support
item.description:
When we make a marriage covenant, we vow “in sickness and in health.” We are committed to being by each other’s side through the highs and lows of life. Perimenopause can be a difficult time in a woman’s life, and it can unexpectedly cause tension and stress in the relationship.

Perimenopause is the “multi-year phase before menopause.” Signs and symptoms of perimenopause usually begin from ages forty to forty-seven and can last from four to ten years. There are drastic changes that occur in a woman’s body and brain.

This is not an exhaustive list of signs and symptoms of perimenopause, but here are some of the changes that a woman can experience to varying degrees of intensity.

  • Hot flashes – a rush of heat from the inside
  • Mood swings – fluctuations in mood
  • Irritability, anxiety, and depression
  • Night sweats – excessive sweating during sleep, causing clothing and bedding to be wet, and not caused by a hot room
  • Insomnia – trouble falling and/or staying asleep
  • Brain fog – change in ability to think, focus, concentrate, and remember
  • Changes in libido – changes in desire to be intimate and feeling attractive and wanted
  • Weight gain – due to hormone changes, a woman burns 200-250 fewer calories per day, making it harder to maintain and lose weight.
  • Increased UTIs and other bladder problems
  • Fatigue – deep exhaustion beyond just feeling tired
  • Joint pain – body aches and other pains
  • Changes in skin – acne, dry skin, increased sensitivity and changes in pigmentation

The age range when signs and symptoms of perimenopause typically occur often happens at the same time in life as other major life changes in a woman’s life. These can include an empty nest, caring for aging parents, losing parents, job changes, and/or starting to have grandchildren.

These major life changes, combined with changes in her body and brain, make stress management, communication, and connection more difficult, causing division and strain in a marriage.

Hormones control metabolism, growth and development, stress response, reproduction, sleep, and mood. Examples of hormones are insulin, adrenaline, estrogen and testosterone, melatonin and cortisol. Hormones control and contribute to many different aspects of a woman’s health.

She may find herself experiencing increased anxiety around everyday tasks – driving, getting ready for the day, sleeping, or simply managing the day-to-day responsibilities that never seemed particularly difficult before.

She may begin to wonder, “What is happening to me?” and even feel like she is going crazy because she cannot understand what is happening in her body and brain. What once felt familiar and manageable can suddenly feel overwhelming, leaving her confused and frustrated, wondering why she no longer feels like herself.

Sometimes perimenopause is missed by doctors and counselors as a major contributor to a woman’s symptoms either because of her age, because she doesn’t meet “enough” of the criteria, and/or because they are not knowledgeable about the extent of its effects. Many women are diagnosed with mood disorders, anxiety, depression, and other mental health diagnoses.

A mental health diagnosis may still be accurate. Still, when it is noted that she is experiencing perimenopause, it helps her doctors and counselors to provide resources and treat it specifically. In doing so, the symptoms of anxiety and depression can decrease.

Some Common Myths of Perimenopause

Hot flashes are the main sign Even some professionals still have this idea that hot flashes have to happen for a woman to be considered perimenopausal. Different women experience different symptoms with varying intensity and frequency.

You can’t get pregnant during perimenopause This is not true, but it can be more difficult to conceive during this time. Symptoms of perimenopause and early pregnancy are similar. The chance of pregnancy doesn’t drop to zero until a woman has not had a menstrual cycle in twelve months.

It’s just physical Husbands can say, “I don’t know what happened, but she has changed over the last few years.” Wives can say, “I don’t know why I am so irritable and miserable. I don’t feel like myself.” Doctors can help with medications but basically say, “It’s just part of menopause. It will be over eventually.”

The ripple effect goes way beyond the physical. When it affects the physical, mental, and emotional, it then affects the woman’s view of herself, her view of her husband, and their relationship.

Love is patient, love is kind and is not jealous; love does not brag and is not arrogant, does not act unbecomingly; it does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered, does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. – 1 Corinthians 13:4-7

This chapter on love does not say to love when others are nice or love when it is easy, but “love is patient, love is kind…”

Communication is key

Before you realize it is perimenopause, you may think, “This is just a stressful time in my life.” It is, but it is compounded by what happens in perimenopause. It needs to be communicated how you both feel and what you are struggling with.

Instead of “You don’t understand me,” say, “I know I have not been myself lately. I am figuring out how to navigate some major changes as a female and really need your patience and support.”

Instead of “What is wrong with you?” say, I have noticed you haven’t been acting like yourself. Is there anything I can do to support you?”

Ways For Husbands to Support Their Wives

First, acknowledge she is going through major changes in her body and brain that are not her fault and are not enjoyable. Just like pregnancy, she is going through changes that make her feel unattractive, insecure, emotional, and irritable. She may feel “old” or like she is “falling apart,” and it came out of nowhere.

Second, communicate with her by asking her how she needs you to support her both physically and emotionally. Work to understand what she is experiencing. Ask for specifics. Ask, “How well did you sleep last night?” “What can I do today to take some weight off of your shoulders?” “What is something that would help you to relax more every week? “

Third, be observant. Asking for what she needs is great, but observing will communicate love to her at a deeper level. Watch for signs of her mood changing, feeling overwhelmed, extra tired, or just feeling “off” and not knowing why. Instead of immediately getting defensive when she is irritable and emotional, realize she may not be feeling well and may need some time to relax physically and emotionally.

Fourth, find ways to relieve her of duties and give her more time alone, with girlfriends or with you, to whatever capacity is doable and makes her feel loved and supported even when she is not acting lovingly.

Fifth, but not least, increase your patience. She may seem so different than the woman you married years ago, but she is still your wife. Take this time to strengthen your communication and affection. If she had a heart condition, cancer, or other medical illness, you would not expect her to “push through it” and do it all anyway.

In addition to patience, be willing to adapt your “normal” way of doing things while she is experiencing the intensity of these symptoms. For example, if her anxiety is higher or she is now experiencing anxiety where she didn’t really struggle with it before, be willing to spend less time at a friend or family member’s house, spend less time away from home so you are with her more, and/or provide more reassurance during other stressful times.

Treatment and Resources

Speak to your gynecologist and/or a menopause specialist about your symptoms. Tell them everything, because what you think might not be connected might be, or be closely related. Counseling can help address your depression, anxiety, stress, and marital tension. You are not falling apart, and you’re not crazy.

The more you know about what is going on in your body and brain, the more you can learn and find ways to manage it healthily. Counseling can and does help. It provides an outlet and can provide you with tools to manage the changes you are experiencing in your relationships and become more aware of your mental health. The more support, the better.

Gynecologists and menopause specialists can assist in developing a plan to treat the most troubling symptoms. There are several medical options. Ask your doctor for all the options so you and your doctor can make the best decision for your health and situation.

The Menopause Society website provides information, including a list of menopause practitioners, and can be searched for your area.

Remember:

  • This is not forever.
  • It is beneficial to reach out for support.
  • Use this time to strengthen your communication of deeper and more personal things with your husband and with God.
  • Your emotions fluctuate, but God’s character does not, and He promises us to “never leave us nor forsake us.” (Deuteronomy 31:8)
  • Your value and worth have not changed.

item.title: Signs You Might Be a Helicopter Mom and What to Do About It
item.description:
It may not be an exaggeration to say that parenting in today’s world is a delicate balancing act that requires wisdom, grace, and a heaping of courage. The balancing act mainly consists of wanting to protect our children from the very real harm and dangers out there, while also trying to help them grow into capable, independent, and faithful adults. For some moms, they may err on the side of what has become known as being a “helicopter mom.”

The instinct to protect those we care about, especially our kids, can morph into something that’s unhealthy. Being a helicopter parent is what happens when that instinct to protect tips into over-involvement.

What is a helicopter mom (or parent)?

Likely due to social media and other factors, the phenomenon of helicopter parenting is more closely associated with moms. It’s important to keep in mind that moms and dads can both be helicopter parents. One way to understand what a helicopter mom or parent is would be to think of it as a parent who constantly hovers over their child’s life. The term comes from how a helicopter circles and hovers over the ground, ready to land when needed.

When it comes to helicopter parenting, it’s about hovering over a child’s life, controlling, monitoring, and intervening excessively at the first sign of difficulty or trouble. This could look like managing your child’s friendships, double-checking every homework assignment, negotiating your child’s conflicts, and shielding the child from failure or disappointments in life.

Helicopter parenting doesn’t seem egregious at first glance. After all, parents are meant to care for their children, and the love a parent has for their child should well up in the desire to protect them. The main challenge with helicopter parenting, which will be explored a bit more later, is that it can prevent a child from being resilient, from developing problem-solving skills, and from developing a sense of independence.

Proverbs 22:6 (ESV) says, “Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it”. This implies giving guidance, and not over-controlling or taking the initiative and the possibility of failure away from the child.

You can imagine a coach training someone and taking over during the game when things start going wrong. You train a team or individual so that they can play the game by themselves, win or lose.

Some Reasons for Helicopter Parenting

There are a few core drivers behind helicopter parenting, and understanding these can help you begin to name and explore some of your own challenges with maintaining a healthy balance.

One core driver behind helicopter parenting is fear and anxiety. This takes many forms and is rooted in several concerns, and it includes a fear of your child experiencing negative consequences. A parent could worry that their child may miss out on opportunities if they fail a class or if their resume is anything short of perfect. College admissions and the job market are competitive, and so the fear is that your child will be excluded unless they perform.

Another core driver for helicopter parenting is anxiety for the well-being of your child. This may not be as future-oriented as concerns for college or work. It could be anxieties about the child getting hurt on the playground or experiencing various social anxieties that lead a parent to view the world as more dangerous than it is.

Parents may be driven to helicopter parenting out of a desire to compete with others or even live through their children. A parent may begin to micromanage their child’s life if they tie their own identity and self-worth to their child’s milestones and achievements. Additionally, peer pressure is also a factor. If other parents are constantly managing their kids, to seemingly great success, that can create guilt and a felt need to try and keep up with them.

Lastly, helicopter parenting may also be driven by overcompensating. If you’re a mom who felt unsupported or neglected in your own childhood, that might drive you to provide the exact opposite experience for your child. In trying to avoid what you didn’t have, it’s possible to then go ahead and do too much, going over the line and becoming overinvolved in your child’s life.

The Impact of Helicopter Parenting on Your Child

There is a difference, though it can be subtle at times, between healthy parenting and helicopter parenting. Healthy parenting leads you to set healthy boundaries that help nurture your own and your child’s well-being. You teach your child godly wisdom and protect them from genuine dangers. There is real risk in the world; your child needs to learn online safety and how to navigate societal pressures. Vigilance is indeed quite necessary.

Helicopter parenting, on the other hand, becomes unhealthy precisely because it crosses the line from guidance and into over-control. As a child grows, the aim is to equip them to handle challenges, but helicopter parenting insulates a child from failure or discomfort.

An example of this difference might be holding a young child’s hand as you cross a busy road versus carrying them everywhere for fear they might trip. One is protection, while the other inhibits genuine growth.

Both the parent and child are negatively affected by helicopter parenting. For the helicopter mom, they will often feel exhausted and beset with constant anxiety. When you feel responsible for every outcome in your son or daughter’s life, you live in constant fear of their failure or harm. You’re finite, and you don’t know everything and can’t be everywhere. Taking on such a role can leave you burned out and frustrated, and it can result in tense family situations.

The child who is exposed to helicopter parenting can be affected in various ways. With fewer opportunities to learn it for themselves, they may become more dependent on others and develop poor problem-solving skills. Without the space to face challenges alone and learn through trial and error, the result may also be low confidence and anxiety.

When a child doesn’t face challenges, they are also deprived of the opportunity for spiritual growth. Difficult circumstances allow us to rely on the Lord for guidance and deliverance, and that opportunity is taken away from the child with a helicopter parent. Being subjected to helicopter parenting can also make a child feel smothered and incapable. Helicopter parenting communicates a lack of trust, and that can be damaging to the child.

Some Signs that You May Be a Helicopter Mom

Moving toward a healthier form of parenting requires that you first recognize the signs of helicopter parenting. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Intervening too quickly If you find yourself intervening at the first sign of your child struggling, whether it’s a difficult assignment or a playground disagreement, that could point to you being a helicopter mom.

Performing their tasks Frequently doing tasks your child could do themselves, like managing their social life, doing their school project, or packing their school bag, is another sign to look out for.

Feeling personally responsible Feeling responsible for their failures or achievements as if their performance reflects your worth as a person and parent, is a potential sign.

The child lacks independence If your child rarely makes decisions independently or seeks your approval for even the small choices they make, that too could also point to you being a helicopter parent.

Stepping Away from Helicopter Parenting

If any of the above signs resonated with you and seemed to describe your parenting style, what then can you do? There are steps you can take to begin moving toward a healthier form of parenting.

You can pray for wisdom and surrender your fears to the Lord. Release your fears to the Lord and ask Him for the wisdom you need to guide your child (Philippians 4:6-7; 1 Peter 5:6-7; James 1:5-8). You can gradually step back by choosing one area to allow your child greater independence, like resolving a minor conflict or managing their homework without your supervision. You don’t have to change everything all at once. Just take one step for now.

As you proceed, focus on giving guidance and not rescuing your child. Instead of solving their problems, ask guiding questions like “What could you do next?” or “How might you handle this differently?” This will teach them to solve their own problems.

A mental and emotional step you can take is to begin embracing failure and imperfection. Mistakes are a part of growth, and you should allow your child to fail in safe and small ways so that they build resilience. Our challenges help us grow stronger, and that’s what the Lord does for us as we go through difficulties (Romans 5:3-4; James 1:2-4).

You can celebrate progress by acknowledging when you let go and when your child takes steps toward greater independence. By focusing on gratitude, you displace fear and create even more room for faith.

Lastly, seek emotional support. Stepping back might trigger anxiety, and you can work through that with help from a Christian counselor. Talk with your counselor to not only lighten the emotional load, but also to recognize patterns of control and helicopter parenting. It is possible to learn to let go in a healthy way and nurture your child toward being the independent, capable adult that the Lord intended them to be.

Call our reception team or fill out an online contact form to schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor. Your journey into a fresh way to parent your children can begin today.

item.title: Walking Through the Grief Process with God
item.description:
Losing a loved one can feel as though the ground has shifted and everything familiar has been sucked into a deep abyss. There is no tidy timeline for the grief process. As believers, we may find ourselves asking questions that seem too much to voice. How do we know that grief and faith can coexist? Is it okay for us to feel this broken when God is supposed to be enough? These are just a couple of questions that Christians may have when faced with something that shakes the very core of who they are—grief.

It is not easy to understand how to move through grief while maintaining honesty and hope. We feel unprepared for this type of broken heart, and sometimes we even lose our ability to speak about the loss, the pain, or our faith. This is where reflection, community, and support make a meaningful difference in how we navigate the grief process.

The Appearance of the Grief Process

No single emotion can define grief. It often comes with a disorienting collection of feelings that includes numbness, anger, confusion, sadness, guilt, and even an unexpected moment of relief. Though many people are familiar with the five stages of grief—denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance—what they rarely understand is that those stages are not linear or orderly.

Grieving people may feel acceptance during one afternoon but wake up the next morning overwhelmed with denial. Grief is on a constant loop, and it arrives in waves without asking permission before showing up. Not only does it affect us mentally, but our bodies are hit with grief in ways that catch us off guard. The most common are disrupted sleep, persistent fatigue, heaviness, and changes in appetite.

Mentally and physically trying to hold onto faith during a hard season can feel disorienting. The unspoken expectation within faith communities that believers should grieve differently can bring a quiet shame that takes root alongside the sorrow. As believers, some expect us to grieve peacefully, quietly, and with a visible trust that God knows what He’s doing. When we exhibit anything other than this, our faith may be questioned and we might feel distant from God.

When the Grief Process Raises Hard Questions About Faith

Grief doesn’t just affect our emotions; it also challenges the very foundation of what we believe. Questions like Why did God allow this? or Where was He? do not reflect a weak faith. In reality, they are signs of an honest faith. Throughout Scripture, followers of God cried out in confusion, pain, and frustration at the silence of heaven. Lamentations is a book that contains various raw, unfiltered stories of grief. In the book of Psalms, we read of many instances of David in the middle of his grief.

As grief intersects with faith, it becomes a place where we can wrestle with God rather than simply rest in Him. This doesn’t mean we have departed from our faith. It means that we are choosing to deepen it by going to Him with our heartbroken questions and emotions. God and faith are not fragile. When we bring honest grief to Him, we stand on a long and sacred history. It is this honesty that carries the weight of trusting that God will be with us in our darkest season.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. — Psalm 34:18, NASB

This verse is steadier than a promise that the pain will be removed quickly. It gives reassurance that we do not face grief alone. God’s nearness to us is not conditional on how composed we are while grieving.

Why Grief Doesn’t Follow a Script

So many times, one of the most isolated aspects of loss is that grief should be finished within a certain timeframe. This can be surrounded by a belief that there is some invisible deadline after which sorrow becomes self-indulgence. Some bystanders may grow uncomfortable with prolonged grief. Even well-meaning people in faith communities can inadvertently communicate that it’s time to move on, trust God more, or look for the silver lining.

The grief process doesn’t cooperate with anybody’s timeline. Complicated grief, prolonged grief disorder, and delayed grief are all patterns in which loss continues to significantly affect daily functioning beyond what feels socially acceptable. This is a human response to real pain and deserves genuine care.

People who are grieving while carrying responsibility for others may find themselves delaying their own grief out of a sense of duty. The result is a quiet absorption of loss while showing up for everyone else. Though the pattern is understandable, it can cause grief to compound over time instead of moving toward healing. Hope does not rush grief, and it refuses to let grief be the ending.

Faith That Becomes an Anchor and Not an Escape

There are times when individuals, especially believers, tend to use spiritual activity as a way to bypass the grief process instead of moving through it. We may find ourselves trying to fill every hour with service, Bible reading, or prayer just because it is a source of comfort. However, this can also become a way of staying busy enough to avoid the harder emotional work that comes with grief. Faith at its best is the anchor that provides a framework for meaning, a community of support, and the relationship with a God who meets us in our most broken place.

Christian counselors are trained to help clients hold both realities at once. They help us understand that the depth of the loss and the steadiness of God’s presence can coexist without minimizing each other. Through this type of integrated care, we can find the transformative grace that shows us we don’t have to choose between grief and faith. The words of Isaiah speak truth to this situation:

He gives strength to the weary, and to him who lacks might He increases power. — Isaiah 40:29, NASB

Being strong in the middle of grief doesn’t always look like composure. Most of the time, it looks like making one phone call, asking for help, or just getting up and trying again. God meets us in the ordinary kind of endurance, the same way that He meets us in moments of spiritual clarity.

Finding Support for the Journey

We don’t have to navigate the grief process alone. It’s not something that we just endure until it passes. Grief counseling, particularly through a faith-informed perspective, can offer a structured and compassionate space to process loss without pressure, judgment, or artificial timelines. In this space your spiritual questions and identity shifts that accompany loss are welcomed and addressed. When we have consistent and professional support during grief, we are given permission to stop managing how our pain appears and just be honest.

When we engage in the right kind of support, we tend to experience a healthier long-term outcome, including renewed purpose and a faith that’s tested but not destroyed. It is not easy work, but it is worth it, and we don’t have to face it alone. Christian counselors who provide grief counseling are trained to create a judgment-free space where loss can be processed at one’s own pace. They also provide tools for identifying grief patterns that may be affecting your relationships, physical health, and overall well-being.

If you have experienced a devastating loss, you’re not alone. Many individuals are navigating faith and the grief process. The first step is to reach out for support. Each of us has a different grief process. Finding care that honors our emotional and spiritual lives matters.

For more information or to be connected with a counselor experienced in the grief process and faith, contact our office. Our reception team can schedule an appointment and get you started on your journey of walking through the grief process with God.

item.title: Early-Onset Dementia Symptoms to Look Out For
item.description:
There are few things more distressing than seeing cognitive decline in someone you love. It is even more difficult to accept when the loved one has not reached old age yet. Early-onset dementia has been known to affect people as young as 30. This means that by the time they reach their mid-60s, the age at which most neurodegenerative disorders begin affecting people, they are already in the advanced stages of decline.

As a loved one, early-onset dementia symptoms might catch you off guard, but if you can identify them early, you will be able to get the support you need. Early assessment often means that you can work with them to develop a plan for the rest of their lives and minimize some of the struggles they will have to face.

The Facts About Early-Onset Dementia

Early-onset dementia is not a disease, but a syndrome. This means that, unlike a disease which has a specific cause, early-onset dementia is merely a collection of symptoms that often do not have a singular cause.

In many cases, early-onset dementia is linked to Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, and frontotemporal dementia. It is currently estimated that cases of early-onset dementia in adults aged 30-64 have more than doubled in the United States in the last few years.

The fact that early-onset dementia is a syndrome, rather than a disease, means that it is difficult to define any risk factors. Studies suggest that genetics, environmental factors, and lifestyle are involved in the development of early-onset dementia.

Many neurodegenerative disorders are genetic, meaning if they exist in a person’s bloodline, there is a risk that they will be passed on from relative to relative. In the case of early-onset dementia, only a physician will be able to provide reliable data on its risk factors and likelihood of occurrence in your bloodline.

Early-Onset Dementia Symptoms

Early-onset dementia symptoms look almost identical to dementia in elderly people, except that they occur in young and middle-aged adults. Dementia of any kind is life-changing, but early-onset dementia affects a person’s family, career, and future.

They become dependent on loved ones at an age where they would otherwise be the provider or leader of their family. Their loved ones must be able to spot early-onset dementia symptoms early and obtain the necessary medical support they need.

Early-onset dementia affects a person’s memory, language and communication abilities, mood regulation, and daily functioning. This affects all the major areas of a person’s life, meaning that their lives will change entirely at some point. As alarming as it sounds, the fact is that they will become dependent on loved ones and medical assistance to function. It is crucial to notice the specific signs that your loved one experiences and intervene as quickly as possible.

Memory Loss That Disrupts Daily Life

If you have seen an elderly person go through cognitive decline, you will know what this looks like. It is repeated questions, frequently forgotten information that they recently learned, and an increased reliance on reminders. They might forget their favorite sports team, the route to work, or their own child’s name. While this can be alarming and hurtful, it is not intentional; they literally can’t help it.

Challenges In Planning or Problem-Solving

One of the areas of life that people struggle with most when it comes to dementia is in the area of finances. Their decreased ability to plan or problem-solve means that their bills accumulate, their salary goes untouched or is abused, and they often find themselves in debt. Besides finances, they might struggle with something as simple as following a recipe or conducting business online.

Difficulty Completing Familiar Tasks

When someone starts struggling with familiar or ordinary things, such as driving their daily route to work or going grocery shopping, it is a sign of cognitive decline. The inability to perform tasks as common and important as these means that they become dependent long before they ordinarily would. Without someone helping them, their quality of life will decline as fast as their cognitive abilities.

Confusion With Time and Place

Part of the daily functions that people with early-onset dementia symptoms struggle with is following time and knowing where they are and why. They might drive to the gym only to be panicked because they don’t know where they are or what they’re supposed to do there. Or they might start getting ready for work late on a Sunday night, hours before they are due at the office.

Trouble With Understanding Images and Spatial Relationships

One of the dangerous aspects of this kind of cognitive decline is struggling with depth perception and having balance that is thrown off. This makes tasks like driving incredibly difficult and dangerous because they cannot judge the speed or distance that other vehicles are traveling at. If your loved one is displaying this particular symptom of young dementia, it’s important to intervene as quickly as possible.

Problems With Speaking or Writing

Dementia affects different hemispheres of the brain, including the area responsible for communication. People with early-onset dementia symptoms regularly lose threads of conversations, have trouble joining in a new conversation, and often trail off because they have forgotten how to finish a thought. Not only does this affect their friendships and social life, but in many cases, it is disastrous for their career.

Misplacing Things and Struggling to Retrace Their Steps

It’s not unusual for a grandparent to misplace an important thing only to find it in an unlikely place. However, when it is your young loved one losing their phone and then finding it in the fridge, it is a different story. When they misplace items, they might start accusing others of having stolen them. They register the item’s disappearance, but can’t remember they were responsible for its last location.

Poor Judgment

When a previously grounded person begins making questionable and risky decisions, it is a sign that they are not thinking as they normally do. People with early-onset dementia usually begin acting out of character. This is most often first seen in their appearance, with grooming and hygiene that deteriorate quickly.

Withdrawal From Work or Social Activities

Part of the dramatic personality changes in someone displaying early-onset dementia symptoms is that they seclude themselves and drop off the social map. This is less noticeable in someone who was never sociable to begin with, but it is often a marked change in the extroverts. They may even decline visits from old friends, which often leads to isolation and depression.

Changes in Mood or Personality

Another clear indicator that someone is going through a major mental health event is that their moods become wildly dysregulated and, at times, their personality changes completely. A normally quiet and nurturing person might turn aggressive, or a naturally confident person might become shy and introverted. Though you might hope that it’s merely a phase, it might be an indicator of something more permanent and infinitely more worrying.

Hope For Their Future

Unfortunately, cognitive decline on this level is rarely curable. The best you can do for a loved one displaying early-onset dementia symptoms is to urge them to meet with a physician and get some tests done as quickly as possible.

You will likely have to help them with future appointments, timekeeping, note-taking, and medication. Another option is arranging support to perform these tasks. Other factors to consider include financial planning, their transportation needs, and potentially seeking legal advice if costly assets are involved in their estate.

Early-onset dementia is a life-changing thing to deal with. However, it is not the end of a person’s life, especially because they are still young. You might have to step up in a way you never prepared for, but you are never alone.

If you are supporting someone in cognitive decline, you also need support. Please consider meeting with a counselor for your own support. You can find one by visiting the online catalog of counselors or speaking with the reception team.

item.title: Intermittent Fasting and Eating Disorders: Can They Coexist?
item.description:
Intermittent fasting (IF) is all the rage at the moment. There are several types of IF, and people see results. But is there a danger in the practice of fasting, especially if you are diagnosed with an eating disorder? What about intermittent fasting if you typically engage in binge-eating behavior?

It’s important to first identify the three common eating disorders (ED) and then explain the pros and cons of intermittent fasting.

What is considered an eating disorder?

An eating disorder (ED) is not a diet someone has taken to the extreme. It is a mental condition that revolves around obsessive thoughts about food. It might be starving oneself to remain thin, purging food out of the system as quickly as possible, or eating tremendous quantities of food in a short time frame.

As many as nine percent of the American population will experience an eating disorder during their lifetime, according to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD). Eating disorders are among the deadliest mental conditions to date, with more than 10,200 people in the United States losing their lives from ED complications each year.

There are three common eating disorders: anorexia nervosa, bulimia, and binge-eating.

Anorexia Nervosa

Anorexia is the preoccupation with one’s appearance and the intake of food. Anorexic individuals may feel disgusted with their bodies or with food. They may attempt to starve themselves for control. Like with other eating disorders, choosing when and what to eat is a form of control. Some people use this to give themselves a sense of security when their lives feel out of control.

The person with anorexia will become a skeleton of their former self, weak, severely underweight, and unhealthy. Without enough nutrients, the body loses fat, muscle, and bone mass. Organ systems will eventually fail, and the heart will stop functioning. This behavior, if left untreated, is fatal. Not only from the inevitable shutdown of the body’s systems, but also the suicide rate for people with eating disorders is high, at around 26%.

Bulimia

While those with anorexia avoid food or eat very little, people with bulimia may consume food normally or in smaller amounts but obsess about ridding the body of the calories as soon as possible. These purging methods can include self-induced vomiting, laxatives, enemas, or extreme exercise. Just as dangerous as anorexia, bulimia destroys the digestive system, the esophagus, teeth, colon, and other systems from the constant purging behavior.

A bulimic may be at their average weight or underweight. With any eating disorder, mood and mental health are also affected. Depression, anxiety, and fear are prevalent. When the body lacks nutrients, the brain does not have enough fuel to operate, and thinking becomes cloudy. As with anorexia, if left untreated, bulimics may need intravenous feeding tubes and oxygen to save them from death.

Binge-eating

Binge-eaters indulge in behavior as if trying to fill a void in their life and in their hearts. A binge-eater may be overweight or obese. Although a binge-eater might plan the binge, they often consume large amounts of food mindlessly in a short period of time. They may eat late at night after their family goes to bed or stop on the way home at a fast-food place to eat hurriedly in their car and dispose of the evidence before they reach home.

While bingeing, the person may not feel the full sensation from their stomach as it stretches. Once the stomach begins to reach fullness in typical eating situations, the brain signals to slow down and stop eating. Food will lose its taste when the stomach is approaching its appropriate limit.

However, during a binge, those signals get lost. The binge-eater can consume thousands of calories and still not feel full. When the binge is over, the person will feel physically and emotionally sick and drained.

This behavior is also physically demanding, with extra fat stores, high blood pressure, high cholesterol levels, and heart attack or stroke risk. Depression, anxiety, guilt, and shame can weigh just as heavily.

What is intermittent fasting?

Intermittent fasting is a break from food to give the digestive system relief. The most common fasting practice is after dinner until breakfast (breakfast = break the fast). For some people, this could mean an eight-hour break. For others, it can mean twelve hours, depending on what time you finish dinner and if you do not have a snack before bed.

Studies show that intermittent fasting can greatly affect insulin resistance, blood sugar levels, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and fat loss.

The most common intermittent fasting plans are 16:8, 20:4, 5:2, and alternate-day fasting.

With the 16:8 plan, the person fasts for 16 hours and eats meals in an eight-hour window. With the 20:4 plan, the fasting window is expanded to 20 hours, and the eating window shortens to four hours.

In the 5:2 plan, the person typically eats five days a week, then cuts back on the amount of food they consume two days a week (generally non-consecutive days). They might fast from food completely with only water or calorie-free drinks or limit their calorie count to a low number.

However, there are some drawbacks to intermittent fasting. Without regular food consumption, the blood sugar level can decrease, causing lightheadedness and moodiness. Many people begin to feel tired during the fast or extremely hungry, especially in the beginning as the change in eating shocks the body.

These are just a few of the IF plans that people use. But should you practice IF if you have been diagnosed with an eating disorder?

Should you practice IF if you have been diagnosed with an eating disorder?

Although intermittent fasting boasts impressive results both medically and with weight loss, practicing IF while dealing with an eating disorder can be devastating. People who suffer from anorexia nervosa need to learn to eat regularly. Depending on the severity of the mental condition, this lack of food (or controlling the fast window) can lead to a downward spiral.

Bulimics tend to fast intermittently, whether they realize it or not, as part of the purging process. They might eat a larger meal, then willfully starve themselves to purge or lessen the “damage” done by the food. The psychological aspect of controlling the timing and food portions is just as strong with IF as with bulimia. If you are diagnosed with bulimia, you should avoid intermittent fasting and speak with a therapist about a treatment plan.

Binge-eaters might be able to intermittently fast, but only under the supervision of a medical professional. It depends on the severity of the condition. Going long periods without eating will lead to a drop in blood sugar and increase irritability.

Some binge-eaters will actually binge once the fast ends. The binge raises the blood sugar (albeit probably much higher than is needed) and provides momentary happiness and relief. Unfortunately, this results in the binge-eater being caught in the vicious cycle again.

A medical professional specializing in nutrition and eating disorders can steer you in the right direction for a treatment plan, not only for your body but also for the mind. You should avoid fasting until you have been given the all-clear from your physician. It may derail your progress.

You should never engage in any extreme eating regimen until you have spoken to your physician and nutritionist. If you have been diagnosed with an eating disorder, consult your therapist. Intermittent fasting does have its benefits, but if it hinders your progress or robs you of your peace, then it is certainly not worth it.

If you do not already have a counselor, contact our offices today. We would love to help you and pray for you as you seek treatment and manage your relationship with food. Appointments are available with the therapists in our practice who have experience with eating disorders.

item.title: Breaking Birth Order Stereotypes
item.description:
In many families, certain roles quietly take shape as children grow up. These roles aren’t assigned on purpose, but they usually follow a pattern tied to what is called birth order. In this order, the oldest child is expected to be responsible and set an example; the middle children learn to adapt and stay in the background, while the youngest child is mostly seen as the fun one, or the eternal baby of the family.

These roles seem like harmless titles, but over time, studies have shown that they do influence what children think about themselves. They then shape confidence, personality, and even the kind of goals people set in life. Some people feel comfortable in the role tied to their birth order, although many others feel like they’re stuck and that it doesn’t match who they really are.

Letting go of these family labels is not something that is easy, but it is possible. The first step is to understand how birth order shapes our identity in the first place.

How Birth Order Affects Parenting

Parents don’t always mean to treat their children differently, but birth order mentalities seem to change parenting style sometimes. That’s because when the first child is born, parents are still new to everything, so they’re usually more cautious. They follow ‘the rules and recommendations’ of ‘good’ parenting.

They read parenting books, ask for advice, and pay closer attention to milestones. The first child grows up in this stricter environment, which begins to set the tone for them to identify with being more responsible.

a second or third child is born, things are usually a bit different. Parents already have some experience now, so they become more relaxed. Now with two kids, they are juggling more, and a tight order gives way to more chaos.

The middle child quickly learns to adjust to the parents, the older sibling, and then not long afterwards, maybe a younger one, too. By the time the youngest child enters a family that already has its routines, there’s less pressure, and parents have become more flexible and a bit more stable.

All of these differences form how each child sees themselves and their place in the family. The impact doesn’t end in childhood. It continues into adult life, guiding behavior and shaping self-esteem.

The Psychology Behind Birth Order

Psychologists have been studying birth order for years, trying to understand how it affects personality. One of the first to look at this closely was the Austro-Hungarian psychologist, Alfred Adler. He believed that birth order influences confidence, independence, and how people act in social situations.

Some studies suggest that firstborns are more likely to become leaders. They learn to take charge early and often try to meet high expectations. Middle children usually become good at building relationships because they spend time trying to fit in and stand out at the same time. Youngest siblings tend to be more relaxed but also work hard to prove themselves because they feel underestimated.

Birth order isn’t everything, but it matters

Birth order doesn’t exactly decide your future, although it has been proven to influence how you see yourself. It affects how you react to stress, how you form relationships, and how you handle goals and failure.

These patterns don’t apply to everyone, but they do influence how people approach challenges, relationships, and personal goals. Knowing more about these patterns helps us understand why we react a certain way in life. Understanding birth order is the first step toward building your own identity.

Firstborns Deal With

Firstborn children usually carry the weight of high expectations. Parents look to them to be the responsible ones. They are asked to help out more and are expected to always lead by example. This kind of pressure starts early and keeps building. For this reason, if you’re a firstborn child, you grow up feeling like you have to be perfect. Many first kids work really hard, feel like they have to take charge, and try to stay in control.

Sadly, this leads to stress and the feeling that they can never relax. Learning to take a step back and accept that it’s okay to also make mistakes can help firstborns feel more balanced and confident in who they are.

What Middle Children Go Through

Middle children face a different kind of pressure, since they aren’t the first, and they aren’t the last. They usually feel like they are just living in the background. Parents may not give them as much attention, and they may not have a clear role in the family.

To feel noticed, many middle children develop strong friendships outside the home, or they learn to adapt and find ways to be different. This builds independence, but can also lead to confusion about where they belong. As a middle child, you will feel stronger when you recognize your importance, ability to connect with others, and stay flexible in changing situations.

What the Youngest Children Struggle With

Youngest children are usually seen as both the easygoing and the spoiled ones. Since parents have relaxed a bit by the time the youngest comes along, they may give them a bit more freedom than they did with the other siblings. At the same time, this also means there are fewer expectations.

This freedom can be fun, but it also comes with downsides. In fact, most youngest children feel like they aren’t ever taken seriously. Even as adults, they’re still treated like the baby of the family, so they always feel the need to prove that they are capable, smart, and independent. As the youngest sibling in a family, you need to know that you grow stronger when you set your own goals and stop waiting for others to see your worth.

Ways to Break Birth Order Stereotypes

This is the way everyone gets strapped into a label they feel like they can never shake. Letting go of these ingrained roles in the family takes time and effort, but it’s worth the effort. You can start with some doable ways to break away from the labels that come with birth order.

Question family roles Ask yourself why you were always seen a certain way and if that role still fits who you are as you get older.

Focus on your strengths Make your own goals based on what you’re good at, not what your family expects from you.

Speak honestly Talk to your family about how you feel about the pressures tied to your birth order.

Try something new Stepping outside your comfort zone and routines helps you grow in ways your family might not expect.

Stop comparing yourself Your path and your success are your own, even if they look different from your siblings’ paths.

Create space for yourself Set boundaries when family expectations get too strong or limiting. Separate personal identity from family expectations.

Follow your passions Get more into hobbies and interests that truly reflect your personality, rather than what you just grew up being expected to like.

Build solid friendships Strengthen friendships with people outside the family to help you grow out of your set family role.

Be open to change Allow yourself to grow and change, even if change surprises others.

Let go of guilt You don’t need to carry the weight of an identity that was assigned to you. Accept that breaking free from that label is healthy and necessary.

Becoming the Person You Want to Be

Birth order plays a big role in shaping how you see yourself, but it shouldn’t define you. You don’t have to fit into a role just because it was handed to you early in life. When you understand how birth order affects your story, you gain the power to rewrite it.

By choosing your own path, you give yourself the freedom to become the person you really are, not just the role you were expected to play. Remember that so much of this role assignment is unintentional and subconscious. Many times, when we challenge it with our family, we can help them be free of these assigned roles, too,

Change is hard, especially when it comes to family. This process is easier said than done. Contact me today for help in growing more fully into your real self without restraint from birth order stereotypes.
