item.title: Self-Care for Anxiety: Finding Peace in the Storm
item.description:
Have you ever found yourself in the middle of a turbulent situation? It might have been a literal storm or a challenging situation that made it nearly impossible to go about life as usual. One common challenge that many people face is anxiety. This is not only the everyday anxiety that affects us all, but crippling anxiety that makes it hard to function. Taking self-care for anxiety seriously is one way to cope well with anxiety in its many forms.

When you’re feeling anxious, it can feel like you’re in the middle of a storm, tossed about by racing thoughts, a pounding heart, carrying the feeling of dread, and a knot in your stomach. Anxiety is a common struggle, but it is one that’s often misunderstood and not attended to properly. Through effective support, you can bring your anxiety under control.

You’re not alone in your anxiety

Being anxious is a deeply human experience. We’ve all felt anxious at one point or another, and there’s a place for anxiety in our lives. Being anxious is a physiological response to danger, and that response can be lifesaving in certain circumstances. When you feel anxious about your first day at work or school, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing if it helps you prepare adequately. Anxiety can even help you as you do something simple like cross a busy street.

Many folks experience anxiety of the kind I’ve described above. It’s one of the many mechanisms in our bodies that allow us to navigate our world successfully. It is helpful to a point as it keeps you alert to your environment and enables you to prepare. However, anxiety can often become something more. Instead of being a help, anxiety can become a burden, keeping you up at night as your mind spins through worst-case scenarios.

This heavier and unhelpful form of anxiety is often referred to as an anxiety disorder. When anxiety no longer helps you, but instead burdens your existence, it is no longer doing what it was meant to. Anxiety disorders come in various forms, and many folks struggle with this more extreme form of anxiety. It can be triggered by anything from social situations, particular animals, or certain daily tasks, including sleeping.

Whatever your situation when it comes to anxiety and anxiety disorders, know that you aren’t alone. People from every background, faith tradition, or season of life face anxiety, and being anxious doesn’t necessarily mean that you’re broken or have weak faith. It is simply a challenging reality that you need support to deal with. One place to start is with intentional self-care.

What is self-care?

People matter, and one of the ways we show that people matter is by caring for their needs. You also matter, and self-care refers to the intentional practices and habits a person cultivates to sustain their mental, emotional, physical, and spiritual well-being. Taking care of yourself requires you to pay consistent attention to what you need so that you can flourish.

Self-care isn’t selfishness, though it’s always good to remember that even the best of the Lord’s gifts to us can be misused. If you’re inclined to ignore your own needs, a change in mindset is needed. Taking care of yourself is a form of faithful stewardship as you care for the mind, body, and life that the Lord has given you. Addressing your anxiety through self-care is a way not to retreat from life, but rather to prepare a way to return to it more fully.

What then is self-care for anxiety? Self-care won’t look the same for everyone, so if you aren’t a bath bomb and scented candle sort of person, that isn’t necessarily what you have to do. If you are, that’s great as a way to find rest and promote restoration. The main thing with self-care is to honestly appraise and understand your needs, then find healthy ways to meet those needs.

When dealing with anxiety, self-care can mean learning your own rhythms, being able to discern and listen to your body’s signals, and disrupting cycles of fear before they take root or escalate. Doing this and nurturing rhythms of life that help to ground you and create a sense of safety will help now and in the long term.

Self-Care for Anxiety – Daily Practices and Long-term Strategies

When anxiety is overwhelming, the temptation may be to try to do a major overhaul of your life so that you nip the anxiety in the bud and can get on with your life. This might seem like a good idea at first, but it can add to the sense of being overwhelmed, and often it isn’t sustainable. Rather, it’s important to have good follow-through on small daily choices, which can have a huge impact on your levels of anxiety over time.

In addition to these daily choices and practices, there are some longer-term strategies that can be implemented to help reduce anxiety and find ways to cope with it. The short and long-term tools work together to help you reduce the intensity and frequency of anxious episodes in your life. Some of the daily practices and long-term strategies for self-care include the following:

Daily Grounding In the morning, before you reach for your phone or iPad, spend five to ten minutes in quiet. Take deep breaths, name three to five things that you are grateful for, and offer up the day to the Lord in prayer.

Movement For many, their lives and work are mostly sedentary. Taking a walk during a work break or getting some exercise at the start and end of your day can help reduce anxiety levels and symptoms. Physical activity improves your mood and metabolizes stress hormones, helping you to calm your nervous system.

Better Sleep Poor sleep and anxiety feed each other. Better sleep hygiene helps anxiety. Try aiming for consistent sleep and wake times, avoiding screens before bed, and having a wind-down routine to help you sleep. These can all contribute to reduced anxiety and better emotional regulation.

Limit Media Consumption An anxious mind is more alert to and can absorb threats more readily. You can protect your mental well-being by setting boundaries around news and social media. Limit the amount of time you spend on media overall, avoid doomscrolling, and seek out balanced news coverage as well as media that also report on the good things happening in our world.

Regulate Your Breathing Anxiety often leads to shallow breathing and your body feeling like it’s in distress. Slowing and regulating your breathing helps to activate your parasympathetic nervous system, which signals safety to your mind and body. When you feel anxious, breathe in for four counts, hold your breath for four, then breathe out for six.

Journal Expressing your anxieties by writing them out helps to give them concrete shape. Externalizing them in this way helps give perspective and distance on those concerns, especially when you combine your journaling with prayer or meditating on a verse from Scripture.

Seek Community Being alone will often amplify your anxiety. Having meaningful and supportive relationships can be a great antidote to fear. The presence of trusted friends or a small group can be a bulwark against unwarranted fears. If you engage in regular conversation with someone like a spiritual director, they can help you pay attention to your inner life and how the Lord is present even in seasons of anxiety.

Sabbath Rest You need to give yourself room to rest, not just physically, but mentally, emotionally, and spiritually. Your weekly Sabbath practice could include stepping away fully from demands, screens, and productivity, and taking time to reflect on the Lord and His goodness. Humbly draw near to Him and seek His peace and rest (Philippians 4.4-7; Matthew 11.28-30).

Therapy Working with a trained and licensed Christian counselor is a useful long-term strategy to address anxiety. Your counselor will help you nurture greater emotional resilience and a deeper spiritual connection as you understand the roots of your anxiety. They can help you challenge the thought patterns that fuel your anxiety and work with you to develop tools to better cope with your anxiety.

This longer-term work won’t eliminate all challenges with anxiety from your life, but it can help you change your relationship with anxiety. Over time, you can become less reactive, more present and grounded, and more deeply rooted in the Lord’s peace that transcends all understanding (Philippians 4:7, NIV).

It is possible to bring anxiety, even the more intense forms of it, under better control. You don’t have to face the storm alone. With support, guidance, and compassionate care, you can begin the journey toward greater peace, healing, and wholeness.

If you’re ready to take the next step, I am here to help. Through counseling, you can explore the roots of anxiety, develop healthier coping tools, and discover a renewed sense of balance and hope. Reach out to my office today to begin your journey toward healing with Joseph Bennett.

item.title: Types of Relationships: Teen Dynamics
item.description:
If you’re a parent to a teen, you probably already know the importance of their relationships. They value friendships, sometimes even over family relationships. It’s not unusual for adolescents to spend enormous amounts of time with their peers and to value the opinions of their friends over anyone else.

Because of this hyperfocus on relationships, it’s important that you, as the loving parent you are, understand the types of relationships your child is in. It’s helpful to understand the unspoken rules and the teen dynamic of these relationships, too. Once you do, you can better determine the healthy and good relationships from the toxic and dangerous ones.

Below are some of the most common relationship dynamics your teen will face.

The Best Friend

A true best friend can be a beautiful gift from God. “A friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17 NIV) isn’t just a poetic verse, but a truth and a benchmark for relationships.

A “best friend” is usually an obvious relationship in any teen’s life. They are mentioned often and are someone your child fiercely defends. And this can be a wonderful thing. When your child has a best friend, they have an advocate, a companion, and someone to hang out with both in and out of school.

Unfortunately, this best friend doesn’t always align with your values. When the best friend is the only voice that matters, the balance of power shifts. If your teens start to mirror everything about the friend, like their language, values, choices, and moods, it’s time to take a critical look at the relationship. Ask your teen some tough questions about morals, values, and behavior, and reestablish your own expectations and set boundaries.

The Frenemy

A frenemy is a “friend” who gives just enough effort for connection to keep your teen engaged but doesn’t necessarily have your child’s best interest at heart. You can spot these kinds of friends when compliments are peppered in sarcasm and when competition is more prevalent than support.

Your teen might feel confused by the contradictions in the relationship. You might too. They might remain loyal to their friend, even defending their action, but it might also shrink their confidence as they are forced to compete or defend themselves.

If you suspect your teen’s friend treats the relationship more as a competition or a battlefield than a friendship, it’s time to talk with your child. Show them that true friendship comes from love. And love shouldn’t leave them anxious or defensive.

The Opposite Gender Bestie

This relationship often starts harmless and platonic. It feels uncomplicated and even exciting, especially compared to the emotional intensity that comes along with dating. Your teen may feel understood by this person in a new and satisfying way.

This is because platonic friends of the opposite gender have a unique perspective on your life that a romantic partner or same sex friend just doesn’t see. Being in an opposite gender friendship can be as comfortable as it is exciting because there is no pressure to label anything, and you get all the benefits of dating without commitment to exclusivity.

These types of relationships are healthy, but they do require some strategy and planning. Emotional closeness without boundaries has a way of slowly shifting. Feelings can develop without a lot of obvious signs. Because the relationship already has emotional intimacy, the romantic bonds can hide behind it and habitual physical closeness.

To keep the dynamic healthy, encourage your teen to keep these friendships in group settings and maintain open conversations with you about where the friendship ends and where feelings begin.

The Habit

Some friendships exist more out of habit than deliberate choice. There’s something special about a relationship with longevity and history, but it’s also possible to outgrow a friendship. Maybe your child had a best friend in elementary school. Though the friendship is familiar, it no longer serves your child, and habit alone isn’t a solid foundation for any relationship.

Teens sometimes stay in relationships long after they’ve outgrown them because change can feel disloyal and off-putting. They might feel an obligation to remain connected even when the relationship no longer encourages growth or lacks other fundamental relationship elements.

As Ecclesiastes tells us, there’s a season for everything. That includes relationships. It’s important to help your teen understand that healthy relationships evolve naturally. Sometimes they grow and deepen, and other times, they fade away.

They may want to pull away from a friendship that doesn’t serve them, or they may have a friend pull away after years of friendship. In either case, they need to understand that this is a natural progression and not necessarily due to a relational misstep.

The Mission

Some teen relationships happen out of a desire to help the other person. Maybe your child sees another child who is sitting alone at lunch or who gets bullied on the bus. And they want to reach out to that child, encourage them, and be their advocate. These are relationships that originate in service and purpose and can be something you’re proud of as a parent. After all, God does call us to bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2 NIV).

While a relationship like this teaches empathy, compassion, humility, and patience, it can also have its challenges. Your teen might sacrifice their own needs or be negatively influenced by the one they are trying to help.

You don’t want to discourage them from helping others, but they need to balance their compassion with self-preservation. To properly serve others, your teen must not act out of guilt or obligation or even a desire for recognition, but with true godly intent.

The Hero

Every teen has someone they look up to. And a lot of times that person is in their friend circle. This person might hold characteristics that your child wishes they possessed. Maybe they are in a leadership role, appear mature or capable, or are successful in their social life.

Admiration itself can be good because it can inspire growth, motivation, and help your teen to set their own goals. But there is a fine line between inspiration and idolization. When admiration turns into idolatry, the relationship can turn from inspiring to toxic and sinful.

Remind your teen that no human should ever be their moral compass. Only God deserves that pedestal. Heroes can teach and inspire, but they cannot give your teen an identity or build their worth because that is found in Christ alone.

The Convenient

Some relationships are simply convenient. Maybe your child has a friend who is in the same classroom or bus route or enjoys the same type of after-school activity. These types of relationships are comfortable, low-maintenance, and that’s perfectly fine. In fact, these easy relationships are the gateway to more meaningful friendships.

The challenge comes when convenience supersedes your child’s discernment. Teens might stay in these easy relationships because it’s easier than thinking through their social choices or because getting out of them might feel awkward.

Help your teen reflect on these relationships. Is this convenient relationship one that they’d keep even if it became inconvenient? If it’s not, it’s important not to let them get too invested, but to enjoy the relationship for what it is, with no expectations. Is this relationship healthy for their spiritual life? If not, they need to prioritize their own growth rather than what is easy.

Teen Therapy

Sometimes teens need a safe space that isn’t home, and they need a listening ear that isn’t yours. They need someone who is trained to actively listen without judgment and who is trained to help them understand their own emotions, relationship dynamics, and the impact on their lives.

Therapy can help your teen learn more about their relationships and how to handle conflict, set boundaries, and recognize the signs that indicate a relationship isn’t serving their best interests.

Therapy isn’t just for your teens. Even rock star parents can feel overwhelmed during the tumultuous teen years. You’re dealing with emotional and hormonal shifts, new social pressures, identity questions, and spiritual growth, all in an intense seven-year period.

If your teen is struggling in their relationships, or you feel unequipped to handle their complex teen years, schedule a session with one of the counselors in our association. These professionals will walk beside you and your teen through all the confusing, stressful, and successful moments that make up the complicated and beautiful time called adolescence.

item.title: How Overlapping Stressors Affect Male Mental Health
item.description:
Many men carry the heavy burden of the expectation to handle everything at once. Work demands are piling up alongside family responsibilities and financial pressures, and male mental health often takes a backseat to these pressing issues.

The problem isn’t the stress that’s present; it’s the way that each area of stress is layered on top of one another, creating a burden that is increasingly difficult to carry. Alone, each of these may be manageable, but together they produce an overwhelming burden that seems unbearable.

Men have been conditioned to approach these situations in a certain way, which creates the challenges. It is an unspoken script of society that says men must manage multiple pressures simultaneously to be considered capable and strong. By admitting that the combined weight feels crushing, they feel as though they are admitting failure.

The reality is that overlapping stressors don’t just add up; they multiply. Relationship strain intensifies when paired with the stress of a demanding job. When health concerns emerge, financial worry deepens. Each area of life affects the others, creating a cycle that seems impossible to interrupt.

Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, NASB

When Work Stress Bleeds Into Everything Else

The line between professional life and personal life becomes increasingly blurred and creates implications for male mental health. Work stress doesn’t stay at work. It follows them through the door, shapes their interactions with the family, and influences their presence in other areas of life.

It’s impossible to feel fully present for a spouse or children when the mind is preoccupied with deadlines and thoughts of job insecurity. They find their minds tethered to unfinished tasks and unresolved problems.

A specific form of tension arises when men feel they are failing in multiple areas of life. They may struggle at work to maintain focus and productivity, and at home, they are emotionally distant and unable to engage with their family.

Christian counselors often see how this division of attention creates a guilt that stacks another form of stress onto the pile. This overlap of stressors suggests that there is no reprieve in sight. Counselors recognize that men feel that addressing one issue appears to neglect another. This results in a feeling of being trapped in a pattern that falls short of expectations for being a good father, husband, and coworker.

For I am confident of this very thing, that He who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus. – Philippians 1:6, NASB

The Hidden Toll of Financial Pressure

It doesn’t matter what area of life it is; money issues will always be present in the decisions. Financial stress isn’t limited to worrying about paying bills or saving for the future. It changes how someone moves throughout their day. It influences choices about what to eat, when to go out to see friends, and when to address health issues that may require spending money.

For many, financial responsibility is deeply tied to their identity and worth. This creates an economic strain that harms their mental well-being. This in turn creates anxiety, depression, or behavioral issues that affect everyday life and being present in the lives of their family.

When this stress overlaps with other pressures, the challenge becomes intensified, and men can face compounded anxiety. When men fear they cannot provide for their families, and that fear intersects with concerns about disappointing loved ones, they find it challenging to maintain stability and preserve dignity.

Christian counselors can easily identify these fears that often go unspoken because men do not want to admit to financial struggle and feel inadequate on top of all the stress they are already struggling with.

This silence about financial problems leads to isolation and prevents men from seeking help. Combined with relationship difficulties or health concerns, there is another level of being overwhelmed that begins to feel paralyzing.

And my God will supply all your needs according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:19, NASB

Physical Health Problems That Compound Mental Strain

Mental well-being and physical health are reciprocally related. When health issues emerge with other stressors, the impact on the mental health of men can significantly intensify. Chronic pain, illness, or declining physical capability doesn’t hide in the shadows.

It affects a man’s ability to work, engage with his family, and maintain a marriage in ways that previously provided him with joy. This loss of physical capability raises questions about identity and the future, as men have allowed it to shape how they are defined.

Health concerns compound existing pressures in complex ways. A man who deals with a chronic condition while managing work stress and family responsibilities must decide how to allocate limited energy. Every activity he engages in will require calculating the physical cost. This consideration adds another layer of complexity to the stressors they face that others may not recognize.

Therefore we do not lose heart, but though our outer man is decaying, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day. – 2 Corinthians 4:16, NASB

Relationship Dynamics Under Pressure

Men facing multiple stressors often see the strain in their relationships. Spouses may notice withdrawal, irritability, or emotional distance before the man recognizes how overwhelmed he has become.

The competing demands of work and finances, along with other pressures, leave little energy for emotional availability for marriage and home life. The result is a painful paradox in which connection and support are needed, but less accessible.

Relationship problems arise from and contribute to other stressors, making it difficult to address one without the other. Struggles at work, combined with a short temper at home, lead to conflict, which is another source of stress.

Financial pressure at home and related relationship strain give rise to economic worry. Health issues that limit intimacy or shared activities create distance between partners. It is a vicious cycle in which one stressor affects another.

Christian counselors observe that this means they underestimate how much these relational rifts compound their overall stress. When emotional support is most needed, its absence makes every other burden heavier.

Addressing the dynamics of the relationship is essential not for the relationship itself, but to create the foundation necessary to address different challenges. It is helpful for men to acknowledge their vulnerabilities with their partners, thereby creating opportunities for shared problem-solving rather than an isolated struggle.

Be devoted to one another in brotherly love; give preference to one another in honor. – Romans 12:10, NASB

Moving Toward Wholeness and Support

With recognition that overlapping stressors require different approaches, there is a path forward to overcome these challenges. Trying to power through the significant pressures simultaneously often leads to a breakdown rather than a breakthrough.

Men who acknowledge that seeking help isn’t a weakness find wisdom as they use practical responses to complex circumstances. Faith is one way to develop a framework for understanding human limitations and dependence on God, and community reflects strength rather than failure.

Moving forward means making choices that may feel counterintuitive. Setting boundaries at work, being honest about one’s emotional capacity, and asking for help with responsibilities may seem illogical when it comes to reducing stressors. But recognizing that mental health isn’t separate from practical circumstances is a small step toward managing one area of stress at a time.

As one area of stress is managed, breathing room enables the management of other pressures. Moving forward doesn’t mean perfection or the elimination of all stress. It involves developing a sustainable way of navigating difficult situations and maintaining connection with oneself, others, and God. This is an acknowledgment of the reality of male mental health challenges and the possibility of finding support and renewed strength for the journey ahead.

Bear one another’s burdens, and thereby fulfill the law of Christ. – Galatians 6:2, NASB
